note: The codex: lore entries the hero unlocks as he discovers them. $ do discover("id") unlocks one; an entry with original or person is unlocked by learning of that original or meeting that person. category must be in categories. text is plain paragraphs separated by blank lines (or a list of paragraphs). quick: true means a quick start that skips its book already knows it. hidden: true keeps a locked entry from showing even as an undiscovered row. Book sessions add entries as the story invents lore; the originals the hero has learned of also appear on their own from content/originals.json. The et_ entries are for the developer sample chapter.

collesanto.title: Collesanto
collesanto.text:
A village on a hill in the middle of Italy, three days' ride from Rome on a good road. The name means holy hill, though no one in the village can say what made it holy.

It grows wheat, barley, figs and a thin red wine. Its people are farmers and shepherds who keep to themselves, pay what the tax collectors ask and say little to strangers. At the top of the hill stands an old villa with its shutters closed, which the village avoids and does not discuss.

the_villa.title: The villa above Collesanto
the_villa.text:
A great house at the top of the hill, shuttered for as long as anyone alive can remember. The shepherds drive their flocks around its wall in a wide curve and will not say why.

Inside, it is dry and clean and strangely empty of small living things. A windowless room in the cellar has a bar on the inside of its door and a bed made up for one who sleeps through the day. There is no name anywhere in the house.

the_hunger.title: The hunger
the_hunger.text:
It is not like appetite. It is a second pulse, patient and enormous, that rises as the night goes on and every time you use what you have become.

Animal blood quiets it, but only for a while. Human blood quiets it far better, and costs something that is harder to name. A starving creature does not choose, and the hunger, if it is left long enough, will choose for you.

the_sun.title: The sun
the_sun.text:
Every story says that the sun kills the dead. You have stood in it, and it has not killed you.

It does hurt. The light lies on you like a fever, and at midday you are weaker and the hunger runs hotter. But you are not ash, and you have no explanation for it. You have learned only that you should not tell anyone.

strix.title: Strix
strix.text:
In Roman folklore the strix is a night bird that feeds on the blood of sleepers, and the word is used for anything that drinks the living in the dark.

The men who came to Collesanto with torches used it of you, and they cried it like a hymn.

et_bloodlines.title: Test Lineage
et_bloodlines.text:
A developer entry that shows how a bloodline is described once the hero has learned of it.

A second paragraph checks that long entries wrap and keep their spacing.

et_place.title: The Test Hill
et_place.text: A developer entry for a place. It unlocks the moment the sample chapter shows the hill.

et_lore.title: A Rule of Testing
et_lore.text: A developer entry in the Lore category. The sample chapter unlocks it only on one branch, so the codex shows both a found entry and an undiscovered one.

et_person.title: The Test Beloved
et_person.text: A developer entry that unlocks by itself when the hero meets the test beloved.

merchant_house.title: The Merchant line
merchant_house.text:
One of the five bloodlines that hold real power in the Senate of Blood. It does not rule by sword or by pulpit. It lends, and it keeps ledgers, and every throne in Rome owes it something.

Its houses hide in plain sight as warehouses, banks and shipping offices. A coven of the Merchant line is a family business with very old partners.

the_veil.title: The Veil
the_veil.text:
The first law of the dead: no human may know. Every other law grows from it. A witness is silenced or mistaken, and a hunter is a danger to everyone.

The Veil is not kept by fear alone. Most of the old ones keep it because they remember what the living do to what they cannot understand.

senate_of_blood.title: The Senate of Blood
senate_of_blood.text:
The Senatus Sanguinis mirrors the Senate of the living. Five bloodlines hold its real power. There were once six, and the sixth is not named.

It settles quarrels between covens, and it keeps the census of the made. It does not forgive a vampire who was never registered.

lictors.title: The Lictors
lictors.text: The Senate's enforcers take their name from the officers who walk before a Roman magistrate with rods bound in red cord. They are patient, they are old, and they are polite until the moment they are not.

collis.title: Collis
collis.text:
The name of the firm, from the Latin for a hill. It deals in oil, wine, ships and debts, and it is run in the daylight by a man the dead cannot match.

A firm leaves a paper trail, and a paper trail leads somewhere. Hide the link and the firm is safer and trusted less. Keep it and the name carries the hill with it.

the_lesser_cup.title: The lesser cup
the_lesser_cup.text: Animal blood will keep a vampire alive, and keep him close to what he was. It leaves him slower, hungrier and weaker in a fight, and some of the old ones say a little sad.\n\nThe made have gone over to it for as long as there have been the made. A great many of them have gone back. It is not a vow that anybody keeps once and is done with.

the_vigiles.title: The vigiles
the_vigiles.text: Rome's night watch, freedmen and slaves in cohorts, who carry buckets and hooks and put out the fires that a city of timber and thatch is forever starting. They are underpaid, underloved and the only people in Rome who walk its streets in the small hours with their eyes open.

the_igniferi.title: The Igniferi
the_igniferi.text: A sect devoted to Vesta, the goddess of the hearth, who hold that fire cleans what the dark has made. They wear grey, they carry a flame in a clay jar that is said never to go out, and they are very patient. They believe the strix, the night bird that drinks blood, is a thing to be burned out of Rome.

the_great_fire.title: The Great Fire
the_great_fire.text: It began in the shops about the Circus Maximus on the night of the full moon of Julius, and the wind from the river carried it up the Aventine and into the old quarters. It burned for the better part of a week, and by the end of it more than half the city lay in ashes.\n\nThe Senate of Blood had known the date for nine days. What the Senate said afterward was a good deal more careful than what it knew.

the_old_quarry.title: The old quarry
the_old_quarry.text: A hollow on the far side of the Esquiline where the first walls of Rome were cut, abandoned for four hundred years. The covens meet there when a matter is too large for any one house. At its far end a bronze door is set into the cliff, green with age, and the General's line keeps its back to it.

general_house.title: The General line
general_house.text: The line of brute strength and war, and the one the Senate uses when it needs a thing done. Its coven in Rome is led by Theron, who marched with Alexander. It answers to Tarrax, the Commander of the Lictors.

scribe_house.title: The Scribe line
scribe_house.text: The line of memory and secrets. Its keepers hold the records of the Senate, of the lines and of the dead, and they have long since noticed what the records leave out. Its coven in Rome meets in the Egyptian quarter under Meritamun.

the_bronze_door.title: The bronze door
the_bronze_door.text: A door of green bronze set into the cliff at the end of the old quarry. It has been knocked on from the inside for as long as anyone in the covens will admit to counting. Cedar bars cross it on the outside.

tarrax.title: Tarrax
tarrax.text: Commander of the Lictors and Firstborn of the General line. He keeps the Senate's peace with iron and does not speak of what is under the cliff.

the_general.title: The General
the_general.text: One of the Six, and the father of the General line. He lay beneath the hill until the door was opened. He asks for a drink, a year and a hat, in that order, and has not yet said what he wants.

surety.title: Surety
surety.text: The oldest custom of the dead. When one of them comes out of the dark, whoever first gives him drink, of their own blood or their own hand, becomes his surety. The Senate asks the ward no questions. It asks them of his surety.

the_watchers.title: The watchers of the Aventine
the_watchers.text: A handful of the vigiles who saw the city burn and saw, in the smoke, something that was not a fire. They have begun to meet in the evenings, in the station yard, with a wax tablet and a list. They do not mean to fight what they saw. They mean to see that somebody wrote it down.

the_keepers.title: The keepers of the hill
the_keepers.text: The oldest way for a human family to serve one of the dead: they hold the house, keep the shutters, know what lies below the stair, and hand the knowledge down. It is an oath that can last for centuries. It makes the family, for as long as it lasts, both a shield and a mark.

the_sack.title: Rome, 410
the_sack.text: Three summers of siege, a gate opened in the dark, and three days in which a very old city learned that it could be entered. It was not burned to the ground, and it was never again what it had been. The Senate of Blood left before the end of the week.

the_cistern_court.title: The court in the cistern
the_cistern_court.text: The Senate of Blood, as it sits at Constantinople: a forest of columns standing in black water, a platform of planks, and a great many old vampires who remember Rome and have agreed not to say so. The Emperor above them rules the day, and believes that he rules everything.

the_great_church.title: The Great Church
the_great_church.text: Justinian's church of the Holy Wisdom, finished in five years on the ashes of the one that burned in the riots. Its dome is lit from forty windows at its foot, so that it seems to hang by a chain from heaven. The court cannot go near it between dawn and dusk.

florence.title: Florence, 1474
florence.text: A republic of bankers under the shadow of a very great family, with a dome that nobody had thought could be built and a river that smells of tanning. It lends to kings, and it keeps the ledgers.

the_court.title: The Court of Florence
the_court.text: The vampires of the city sit as a court under a Prince, not a Senate. The Prince keeps the peace and the Merchant house keeps the purse, and neither says out loud which of the two is the more important.

san_custode.title: San Custode
san_custode.text: The guardian saint of the hill, who never ages, put out a fire at the mill and walked in the plague. He sleeps, they say, in a cellar under the shrine, and wakes when the hill is in danger. Nobody can say where the story began.

blood_licence.title: The licence of the Purse
blood_licence.text: Within the walls of Florence no vampire may feed on a citizen without a numbered brass licence from the Purse. It is one citizen a month, taken with consent or without harm, and the fee goes to the bank. The Prince keeps the peace and the Purse keeps the tally.

pazzi_medici.title: The Medici and the Pazzi
pazzi_medici.text: Two great banking houses and a quarrel that grows each year over alum, a will and a Pisan archbishopric. Some in the court find it useful to keep it warm.

priestess_line.title: The Priestess line
priestess_line.text: Old, proud and unhurried. Its princes hold courts rather than senates and rule by knowing what everyone owes.

the_purse.title: The bank of the Merchant house
the_purse.text: A plain door and a bronze ring, with a counting floor of forty tables, a licence office and a strong room under the street. It is one of the six great houses of Florence and has never been seen to fail.

banca_del_colle.title: The Banca del Colle
banca_del_colle.text: The house on the Via Porta Rossa with a green hill on its sign. It is open from the third hour to the ninth, by day, and run by a man who sits in the sun. The guild requires a new bank to make its first great contract in the open, at noon, in the Mercato Nuovo.

the_velati.title: The Velati
the_velati.text: The Veiled Watch, begun by a vigil of the Aventine who wrote down what he saw. They keep a book, in a shorthand passed from hand to hand, and send agents to watch the old blood. Their rule is to see, to write and not to interfere. They mark their letters with a closed eye.

the_roll.title: The Remembrancer's roll
the_roll.text: A calf bound book, ruled in red, in which every debt, favor and secret of the court at Paris has been entered for two hundred and fifty years in one small black hand. Most of the long right column is owed to a single house in Amsterdam.

berengaria.title: Berengaria
berengaria.text: The Prince's Remembrancer. She is the oldest vampire at the Florentine court that you have met, and says that her office is remembering what everyone else is anxious to forget.

nanni.title: Nanni
nanni.text: A seller of thread in the Mercato Vecchio who has been a small customer of the Merchant house for longer than the books go back. He does not look at you quite the way other people do, and you cannot afterward say why.

the_old_mint.title: The old mint
the_old_mint.text: Gold that has been refined so many times by so many careful hands that it is purer than anything newly struck. Somebody in Florence is paying for a great deal with it, and the coin smells of a house in which no fire has been lit for a very long time.

the_merchant.title: The Merchant
the_merchant.text: One of the Six, and the father of the Merchant line. He sold thread in the Mercato Vecchio for longer than the books go back, and nobody could afterward say what color his eyes were. His gift is shadows: he gives a man's memory of his face to his shadow, and the man goes away with it.

paris_court.title: The court at Paris
paris_court.text: The vampire court of Florence followed the Medici queen over the Alps and settled in Paris, where it has grown decadent on pastry and politics. The Prince keeps the peace, the Merchant house keeps the purse from Amsterdam, and nobody has asked the court's opinion of the king.

the_barrieres.title: The Wall of the Farmers General
the_barrieres.text: A ring of fifty toll houses joined by a wall, built in the last four years to catch wine, salt and firewood on their way into Paris. It is of no use against an army and a great deal of use against a cart. The people say that the wall that walls Paris makes Paris murmur.

the_press_trade.title: The book trade of the Latin quarter
the_press_trade.text: Paris has more printers than the police can follow: licensed houses with a royal permission, houses with a tacit one, and houses that print under the name of a town in Switzerland. A shop is raided on the word of a rival or an informer, and a printer who is taken goes to the Bastille.

the_peace.title: The Prince's Peace
the_peace.text: The old agreement of the court at Paris, brought over the Alps from Florence: no vampire hunts in the open, no vampire quarrels in the streets, and every grievance goes to the Prince. The young think it is a cage. The old think it is the reason that anyone is still alive.

the_lictors_of_paris.title: A Lictor in the rue des Prouvaires
the_lictors_of_paris.text: The Senate in Rome has sent a Lictor to Paris on a matter of the court's roll. He has taken a room over a cutler's, wears a plain brown coat, and asks courteously after a certain kind of Roman face.

the_estates_general.title: The Estates General
the_estates_general.text: The king has called the three estates, clergy, nobility and everyone else, to meet at Versailles in May for the first time in a hundred and seventy five years. The Third Estate has been promised as many seats as the other two together, and is reading a great deal.

the_cahiers.title: The cahiers de doléances
the_cahiers.text: Every parish and every guild in France has been asked to write down its grievances for the Estates. In the Latin quarter the printers are making the blank forms by the thousand.

friends_of_the_blacks.title: The Friends of the Blacks
friends_of_the_blacks.text: A society of Paris writers and bankers, founded in the year before he woke, that asks the kingdom to end the slave system of the colonies. It has more learning than money and more friends in London than in Paris.

the_quarries.title: The quarries under the hill
the_quarries.text: The old stone workings from which Paris was built run for leagues under the left bank, dry, cool and unmapped. The city has lately been emptying the churchyard of the Innocents into them, by night, a million bones in neat ranks.

the_cadets.title: The Cadets
the_cadets.text: The young vampires of the faubourg Saint-Antoine, made in a hurry by a great many different hands and left to learn the rules from one another. They meet in a brewery cellar in the rue de Charonne and wear a scrap of lilac.

the_reveillon_riot.title: The Reveillon riot
the_reveillon_riot.text: On the 27th and 28th of April 1789 a crowd of the faubourg Saint-Antoine burned the effigy and then the house and works of a wallpaper maker who was said to have wished the people to live on fifteen sous a day. The Gardes Françaises fired into the street. Nobody agrees on the number of the dead.

the_bastille.title: The Bastille
the_bastille.text: The old royal fortress and prison at the east end of the faubourg Saint-Antoine, eight round towers with a few prisoners in them and a great deal of powder. On the 14th of July 1789 the people of Paris took it in an afternoon.

the_great_fear.title: The Great Fear
the_great_fear.text: In the last days of July 1789 a rumor of brigands, said to be hired by the nobility to cut the green corn, ran across France faster than a rider could carry it. A hundred thousand villagers rang the tocsin and took up arms against an enemy that was not there.

the_declaration.title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
the_declaration.text: Seventeen articles passed by the National Assembly on the twenty sixth of August 1789. It says that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, and it does not say which men.

the_innocents.title: The Innocents
the_innocents.text: The oldest cemetery in Paris, six hundred years of the dead in a single walled yard. It was closed in 1780 and has been emptied, a cart a night, into the quarries beyond the Barrière d'Enfer.

the_october_days.title: The October days
the_october_days.text: On the fifth of October 1789 the market women of Paris marched on Versailles in the rain, asking for bread. On the sixth they brought the king and queen back to the Tuileries, with the baker, the baker's wife and the baker's boy as their cry.

the_avignon_account.title: The Avignon account
the_avignon_account.text: A purse of gold sent four times a year from the Prince's house to a town in the south, in the name of a Lady who sleeps, and a letter that comes back.

the_third_cellar.title: The third cellar
the_third_cellar.text: The deepest cellar of the Hotel de Saint-Aubin, older than the house, closed by a steel door with a grille. The court calls it the Cellar and does not say what is in it.

the_national_lands.title: The national lands
the_national_lands.text: The Church's property, put at the nation's disposal in November 1789 and sold off by the district offices from the winter of 1790. The Valere house was offered a convent in the rue de Vaugirard.

the_declaration_of_the_blood.title: The Declaration of the Blood
the_declaration_of_the_blood.text: Seven articles drawn up by the Cadets: no rule by terror, no hunting within the walls without a vote, a seat for the young.

the_senate_letter.title: The Senate's letter
the_senate_letter.text: A letter under the wolf seal, asking what became of the Lictor sent to Paris and what the hero means to do about the boy.

the_federation.title: The Champ de Mars
the_federation.text: The drill ground dug out by the whole of Paris in June 1790 for the Festival of the Federation, with the Altar of the Fatherland at its centre.

the_flight_to_varennes.title: The flight to Varennes
the_flight_to_varennes.text: The king's flight from the Tuileries on the night of the twentieth of June 1791, stopped at Varennes the next evening.

the_republic.title: The word Republic
the_republic.text: In June 1791 a word that no respectable house in Paris had yet printed.

inspector_garnier.title: Inspector Garnier
inspector_garnier.text: The police inspector who kept a file on every printer in the quarter, and who came to the shop door on the night of the king's flight.

the_champ_de_mars.title: The seventeenth of July
the_champ_de_mars.text: The shooting at the Altar of the Fatherland on the Champ de Mars, where the National Guard fired on the crowd signing the Cordeliers' petition.

the_key_of_the_cellar.title: The key to the third cellar
the_key_of_the_cellar.text: A small bright steel key, newly cut, to the grille of the third cellar of the Hotel de Saint-Aubin. The Prince offered it in the summer of 1791 to the one person he could find who would not kneel.

the_constitution_of_1791.title: The Constitution of 1791
the_constitution_of_1791.text: The first written constitution of France, accepted by the king on the fourteenth of September 1791. It made him a king under the law and closed the Assembly that wrote it.

the_declaration_of_war.title: The war of 1792
the_declaration_of_war.text: France declared war on the king of Bohemia and Hungary on the twentieth of April 1792. It was voted by acclamation, and went badly from the first.

the_swiss_guard.title: The Swiss Guard
the_swiss_guard.text: Some nine hundred men of the Swiss regiments, in red coats, who held the Tuileries for the king in the summer of 1792.

the_tenth_of_august.title: The tenth of August
the_tenth_of_august.text: The storming of the Tuileries in 1792. The tocsin began at midnight, the Marseillais and the faubourgs took the palace in the morning, and the king was suspended.

the_second_slate.title: The second line
the_second_slate.text: A passage that the Lady's hand began to write in August 1792, after a long silence. It names a Sunday in September and a house in the rue de Vaugirard.

the_second_of_september.title: The second of September
the_second_of_september.text: The first of the prison massacres of 1792. Paris, with Verdun under siege and the barriers shut, killed over a thousand prisoners in four days, beginning with priests at the Abbaye and the Carmelite house in the rue de Vaugirard.

the_abbaye.title: The Abbaye
the_abbaye.text: The old prison of Saint-Germain-des-Pres, where on the night of the second of September 1792 a self appointed table under a man named Maillard judged the prisoners one by one, by lamplight.

the_twenty_first_of_january.title: The twenty first of January
the_twenty_first_of_january.text: The day in 1793 when the king, who had been tried by the Convention and condemned, was put to death in the Place de la Revolution at about ten in the morning, in a fog, under a roll of drums.

the_third_slate.title: The third line
the_third_slate.text: A passage that the Lady's hand wrote on the night before the king's death. It names a man who is to stand up from under the knife, and says nothing of what is to be done with him.

the_keepers_of_paris.title: The keepers of Paris
the_keepers_of_paris.text: The Valere house in the rue Saint-Jacques, printers, who have kept the hero's books and his haven since the court came to France. The post passes with a ring of keys and a form of words that is older than the house.

the_law_of_suspects.title: The Law of Suspects
the_law_of_suspects.text: A decree of the seventeenth of September 1793 that ordered the arrest of everyone who might be thought an enemy of the Republic: nobles, their kin, those refused a certificate of civism, and those who could not account for their means. The Tribunal and the Section lists did the rest.

the_twenty_first_of_brumaire.title: The twenty first of Brumaire
the_twenty_first_of_brumaire.text: The eleventh of November 1793, in the Year Two. A sitting of the Tribunal ran late, and the last cart came to the Place of the Revolution by torchlight. What the crowd saw there is still told in Paris, and not agreed.

the_ninth_of_thermidor.title: The ninth of Thermidor
the_ninth_of_thermidor.text: The night of the twenty seventh of July 1794, in the Year Two, on which the Convention turned on its Committee and the Terror ended in a day. The Commune rang the tocsin, the Guard went over by the stair, and in Paris nobody was able to say, until the carts had gone, which paper was the true one.

the_priestess_awake.title: The Lady of the third cellar
the_priestess_awake.text: The Priestess line's eldest, who slept in the rosemary under the Hotel de Saint-Aubin and wrote the court's doings on a slate. She woke in the small hours of the eleventh of Thermidor, in the last days of July 1794, and released the Prince. She has said that she has a great deal to attend to, and that it will keep.

the_crescent_city.title: New Orleans, 1859
the_crescent_city.text: A port built on a bend of the river, lower than the water that feeds it, so that nothing is buried and nothing is quite dry. The largest cotton market in the world and the largest market in people in America. The streets are French and Spanish, the money is English and Northern, and every house in it has been paid for.

the_second_empire.title: The Second Empire
the_second_empire.text: The nephew of the first Napoleon, elected President in 1848 and made Emperor four years later. He rebuilds Paris with straight boulevards and gas lamps and moves the people who lived where they run. The printing trade is licensed, and watched, and mostly kept.

the_river_covens.title: The river houses
the_river_covens.text: The vampires of the lower Mississippi keep to the old plantation families, and keep their own courts, and have kept out of the Senate's reach for a hundred years. They are said to be proud, patient, and very well informed.

the_free_people_of_color.title: The free people of color
the_free_people_of_color.text: A class of free men and women, many of them property owners and tradesmen, who have lived in New Orleans since the Spanish. They have their own schools, churches and societies. Every year the law of the state grows narrower for them.

the_cotton_economy.title: Cotton and the slave economy
the_cotton_economy.text: The fortune of the age. Every bale on the levee is the work of enslaved people, and every loan against it is written on the security of persons. A man who invests in it may never see what he has bought, which is the point of the arrangement.

the_st_louis_exchange.title: The Exchange and the yards
the_st_louis_exchange.text: The great domed hall in the St. Louis Hotel where bills on Liverpool and Havre are cried every day, and where people are sold at auction under the same roof. The dealers' yards on Baronne and Gravier Streets keep an inventory for private sale, behind a painted board and a lamp, as respectably as any hardware shop. The law forbids selling a child under ten apart from its mother.

the_compact_of_the_river.title: The Compact of the River
the_compact_of_the_river.text: The old rule of the lower Mississippi houses: no turning in another's parish without leave, no feeding on another's people, no quarrel carried out of doors. It is a hundred years old, and has held because it has never yet been tested by anything larger than pride.

the_election_of_1860.title: The election of 1860
the_election_of_1860.text: Four candidates, a divided country, and a Southern press that has told its readers for a year what will follow if the Illinois lawyer wins. In New Orleans the torches are lit before the polls are closed.

the_secession_of_louisiana.title: The secession of Louisiana
the_secession_of_louisiana.text: A convention at Baton Rouge votes the state out of the Union in January 1861. New Orleans fires a salute of twenty one guns and flies a blue flag with one star.

the_senate_of_blood_now.title: The Senate, now
the_senate_of_blood_now.text: No longer a hall. A correspondence of Residents in nine cities, a Secretary who reads and a very few who decide. It asks every house on the continent to do nothing in the war that cannot be explained afterwards as a war.

the_free_people_of_color_law.title: The free colored registration law
the_free_people_of_color_law.text: After secession the parish requires free people of color to register and to carry their papers, liable at any time to be asked how they come by them. The free families of the Bayou Road begin to look for doors.

the_blockade.title: The blockade
the_blockade.text: In the last week of May 1861 a Federal sloop of war takes station off the Passes. The cotton on the levee has nowhere to go and the river stops.

the_northern_houses.title: The Northern houses
the_northern_houses.text: A few old vampires of the North, made in the days of the colonies, who have decided that a country can be made to behave. They would like a friend in the lower river. Mr. Crane is, by their account, not that friend.

the_river_houses.title: The river houses
the_river_houses.text: Seven vampire houses on the lower Mississippi, bound by the Compact of the River. They have been rich for a hundred years and have never had to learn how to be poor.

the_native_guards.title: The Native Guards
the_native_guards.text: A regiment of free men of color, raised in the spring of 1861 and drilled in blue coats on the Plains of Mexico. They are the only free men in Louisiana to be given a gun by their government.

the_fall_of_new_orleans.title: The fall of New Orleans
the_fall_of_new_orleans.text: On the morning of 24 April 1862 a Federal fleet passes Forts Jackson and St. Philip in the dark and anchors off the levee the next day. The Confederate troops withdraw, the city is left to its mayor, and the Union flag follows within days.

the_burning_of_the_cotton.title: The burning of the cotton
the_burning_of_the_cotton.text: As the fleet approaches, the city's cotton is rolled onto the levee and burned by order, with steamboats and an unfinished ironclad set alight on the river. Sugar and molasses run in the gutters, and the poor of the Irish Channel gather it.

the_occupation.title: The Occupation
the_occupation.text: From May 1862 the city is governed by General Butler, who cleans the streets, feeds the poor from army stores, hangs a man for tearing down the flag, and is hated by the best families. Many of the old houses leave for the upper river.

the_oath.title: The oath of allegiance
the_oath.text: The Occupation requires residents to register and swear to the United States. Foreigners may register with their consuls instead. Those who refuse have their property inventoried.

the_contraband_camps.title: The contraband camps
the_contraband_camps.text: As the army moves up the bayous, people from the sugar parishes walk to the Union lines at Camp Parapet and elsewhere. In September 1862 the free men of the Native Guards are mustered into Federal service.

the_new_general.title: The new General
the_new_general.text: In December 1862 General Butler is recalled and replaced by General Banks, a Massachusetts politician sent to be liked. The army prepares to move up the river toward Port Hudson.

port_hudson.title: Port Hudson
port_hudson.text: A Confederate fortress on a bluff above the Mississippi, held under siege by Union forces from May to July 1863. Its fall, with Vicksburg, opens the whole river.

the_hospital_boats.title: The hospital boats
the_hospital_boats.text: During the siege of Port Hudson steamboats carry surgeons, ice and nurses upriver from New Orleans to the landing at Springfield, where the wounded are laid in rows in a field.

the_river_houses_in_the_war.title: The river houses in the war
the_river_houses_in_the_war.text: Southern vampire houses follow their states into the war and hold part of the trenches at Port Hudson. They do not fight like soldiers, and they do not forget who has helped them.

the_river_opens.title: The river opens
the_river_opens.text: Vicksburg falls on 4 July 1863 and Port Hudson on 9 July. The whole Mississippi is in Union hands, and New Orleans is joined to the upper valley again.

the_first_open_summer.title: The first open summer
the_first_open_summer.text: With the river open, shuttered warehouses are sold for almost nothing and merchants of every kind come back to the Levee to rebuild their trade.

the_ice_trade.title: The ice trade
the_ice_trade.text: Ice shipped from Boston in sawdust is worth more than cotton in a Gulf summer. Whoever holds the first cold warehouse on the open river holds a good deal of the city.

the_mobile_house.title: The Mobile house
the_mobile_house.text: A small house of the Gulf coast, beaten at Port Hudson and cut off by the blockade. It wants the Compact to name it a house in its own right.

the_returning_guards.title: The returning Guards
the_returning_guards.text: After Port Hudson the wounded of the Native Guards come down the river by hospital boat to the Treme, where the free families wait for them at the landing.

the_free_labor_system.title: The free labor system
the_free_labor_system.text: General Banks orders that freed people on the sugar estates be paid a small wage and bound to the plantation for a year by passes. Many call it slavery under a new name.

the_teche_house.title: The Teche house
the_teche_house.text: A river house of the Teche country, led by the Delorme brothers, who do not wish the Compact written again and will pay in iron to prevent it.

the_labor_contracts.title: The labor contracts
the_labor_contracts.text: Contracts read aloud in the yards of the sugar estates in winter 1863 set wages, passes and a year of work. Some estates add schools or land, most do not.

the_school_in_the_treme.title: The school in the Treme
the_school_in_the_treme.text: Honorine Armand keeps a school for the children of the free families and the freed, supported by a society of the Treme, and the lamp in its window is lit every night.

the_new_state_government.title: The new State government
the_new_state_government.text: In March 1864 a Governor is sworn in at Lafayette Square under the Army's protection, elected by a small number of voters. It is a government of the State and not yet a settled one.

the_atlantic_houses.title: The Atlantic houses
the_atlantic_houses.text: The vampire houses of Boston and New York keep to a few old rules of their own and write to each other in small neat hands. They did not take sides in the war and are now thinking about what comes after it.

the_chapter_of_the_river_houses.title: The Chapter of the river houses
the_chapter_of_the_river_houses.text: The river houses meet in Chapter at Belle Rive to read the Compact aloud and vote on a breach with a white stone and a black. A fine is paid in silver and sometimes in a seat.

the_petition_of_the_free_men.title: The petition of the free men
the_petition_of_the_free_men.text: In early 1864 the free men of color of New Orleans draw up a petition to the President asking for the vote, on the grounds of taxes paid, houses owned and a regiment raised.

the_free_state_convention.title: The convention of 1864
the_free_state_convention.text: A convention at the Mechanics' Institute writes a new constitution for Louisiana whose first article abolishes slavery. It is voted on in September.

the_gulf_house.title: The Gulf house
the_gulf_house.text: The vampires of the lower Gulf coast around Mobile have never had a house of their own at the Compact table. Gaspard Fontenot asks for one in the autumn of 1864.

the_atlantic_compact.title: The Atlantic Compact
the_atlantic_compact.text: Elias Thorne and H. Crane propose a common law and a common court for the houses of the North and the South, with a seat for each house that signs.

the_ice_company_warehouse.title: The ice company warehouse
the_ice_company_warehouse.text: A brick shed on the Levee with a deep cellar holds hundreds of tons of ice cut in New England. It is the only place in the city that stays cool in September, and it has enemies.
